notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to both Moses and Aaron to begin a new counting of the Levites. An earlier count included all male Levites from one month old, but this new count focused on those ready for active labor. Aaron was included with Moses because the priests had to oversee every part of this sacred work.

God told Moses and Aaron to count the men of the Kohathite clan who were between thirty and fifty years old. Kohath was counted first because his family carried the most sacred objects, even though Gershon was the older brother. Men in this age range had the physical strength and maturity needed for heavy, holy work. Joining this service was described like entering an army, showing that serving God is an orderly and serious task.

The Kohathites were given the special duty of caring for the most holy things inside the sanctuary. This included the ark of the covenant, the golden lampstand, and the altars. God assigned specific duties to each group so that everyone knew his place and there would be no jealousy or confusion.

When the camp was ready to move, Aaron and his sons went in first to cover the ark of the Testimony with the inner curtain. Over this veil they placed a tough leather covering to keep out rain, and over that a cloth of solid blue before putting in the carrying poles. The priests were allowed inside because the pillar of cloud had lifted to lead the camp. The bright blue covering on the outside signaled to everyone that the ark was the throne of God.

The priests spread a blue cloth over the table of the Presence and set its plates, cups, and bowls on top. The sacred bread remained on the table even during the march, showing that God's provision for his people never stopped. They covered everything with a scarlet cloth, added a layer of protective leather, and inserted the carrying poles.

Aaron and his sons covered the golden lampstand and all its lamps, wick trimmers, trays, and oil jars with a blue cloth. Then they wrapped the lampstand and its tools in fine leather and placed the bundle on a carrying frame. Unlike the ark and table, the lampstand received only two layers of cloth and leather.

The golden incense altar was covered with a blue cloth, wrapped in fine leather, and fitted with its carrying poles. This altar was plated with pure gold and used for burning sweet incense in the Holy Place. God required even this smaller altar to be shielded from weather and sight before it was moved.

The priests gathered all the other utensils and garments used for serving in the sanctuary and wrapped them in a blue cloth. They covered the bundle with fine leather and set it upon a carrying frame. Every single item used in worship was treated with the highest care and respect.

The priests cleared the ashes from the bronze altar in the outer courtyard and spread a purple cloth over it. They placed all its firepans, forks, shovels, and bowls onto the altar, wrapped everything in leather, and inserted its poles. The purple cloth set this outer altar apart from the furniture inside the tent, which used blue cloths.

Only after Aaron and his sons finished packing the sacred objects were the Kohathites permitted to come and carry them. The Kohathites carried the items by the poles and were strictly forbidden to touch the holy objects directly, or they would die. This boundary taught the people deep reverence and protected them from God's judgment.

Eleazar, Aaron's oldest surviving son, was given personal charge of the lamp oil, fragrant incense, daily grain offering, and anointing oil. He also oversaw the entire tabernacle and supervised the Kohathite workers. While the Levites bore heavy physical loads on their shoulders, Eleazar carried the heavy spiritual duty of making sure nothing was lost or neglected.

The Lord gave a solemn warning to Moses and Aaron to make sure the Kohathite clan was not wiped out. If the priests became careless and left holy things uncovered, the Kohathites would die when they arrived to pick them up. Leaders bear a serious responsibility to protect those under their care from stumbling into fatal mistakes.

To keep the Kohathites safe, Aaron and his sons had to enter first and assign each man his exact burden. No worker was left to pick his own task or wander around the sanctuary furnishings on his own. Clear order and watchful direction prevented fatal errors in God's presence.

The Kohathites were forbidden even to look at the holy objects for a single second while the priests packed them, or they would die. The phrase for this moment means as brief as a single gulp. God kept these items hidden under the old covenant to guard his holiness and keep his people from treating sacred things casually.

God next commanded a census of the Gershonite clan, counting men from thirty to fifty years old. Like the Kohathites, these men entered active service to do the physical work needed for the Tent of Meeting. Even though Gershon was Levi's firstborn son, his family was counted second because their duties involved the tabernacle's fabrics rather than the most sacred furniture.

The Gershonite clans were given the responsibility of packing and transporting the various curtains, coverings, and hangings. Though their job involved heavy drapery rather than the golden furniture, their labor was necessary to God's sanctuary. In God's house, every assigned task is important and should be done with a willing heart.
